summary: Round 7's two majors are genuinely closed and the fixes do not appear to have created a third major. R7a: closeDelegateQuietly clears the flag with a one-shot Thread.interrupted() before delegate.close() and does not restore it; nothing on that thread reads the flag after the call returns (closeDelegateQuietly is the last statement of drainForever's finally), so the clear masks nothing on this thread and NOT restoring is right -- the committer is terminating and has no caller to carry the flag to. R7b: the new order in drainForever's finally (terminated = died; stop(); failAll(drainRemaining(), terminalFailure()); then LOG + closeDelegateQuietly()) is correct. Nothing is failed too early -- stop() is under the same lifecycle monitor submit() enqueues under, so after it returns the queue is stable, and the in-flight batch was already failed by drainLoop's own catch. Nothing is drained twice -- LinkedBlockingQueue.drainTo is atomic and close()'s own drain runs only after committer.join returns. terminalFailure() is still correct for callers drained before the delegate close, because `terminated` is assigned one statement earlier and both branches of terminalFailure() are reachable and correctly discriminated (died == null only when close() drove the exit, which I checked by exhausting drainLoop's three return sites). catch (Throwable) in closeDelegateQuietly cannot swallow anything that should terminate the JVM: an uncaught Error out of a VIRTUAL thread's run body never terminates the JVM anyway, so the change converts a stderr dump into a structured ERROR log and is strictly better; and the pre-fix behaviour it replaces (an Error escaping the finally and skipping failAll) is exactly the R7b defect. Cost: no new object-store request anywhere. LocalSequencer.commitAll -> CommitLog.commitAll -> commitSubmissions issues exactly one putIfAbsent per batch (plus one get per lost race, which is contention, not fleet size), CommitLog.commit was already a one-element commitSubmissions so the LocalSequencer rewrite is behaviour-identical for the single-request case, and no production implementor of the new commitAll primitive loops per request. The idle path issues nothing (queue.take() gates the window). The cost equality the task demands is asserted, not approximated: sixPodsCommittingInOneWindowCostONEPutNotSix pins puts() == 1 through CountingBinStore. The baselines/review.txt rounds:M4.7 argument is accurate on every mechanism claim I checked against the tree (drainLoop's interrupt re-arm at :334, BoundedLock.takeOrFail's tryLock(bound, NANOSECONDS) throwing on the flag, and the pre-fix catch (Exception) letting an Error abort the finally before failAll), and its classification of the sleepFor minor as a cost defect is sound: with the old lower-bound-only assertion a constant () -> Thread.sleep(200) behind a 5 s configured interval was 25x the PUT rate and left the tree green, which is the NFR-1 dimension this class exists to protect. Three minors below; none blocks, and per review.md fixing them is permitted and usually wrong.

findings.title: close() interrupts the committer unconditionally, including while the committer is inside its own lease release -- and R7b's reordering is what makes that window reachable from a caller
findings.failure_scenario: closeDelegateQuietly()'s Thread.interrupted() at :300 is a ONE-SHOT clear; close() at :424 calls committer.interrupt() with no regard for where the committer is. Interleaving: the committer dies abnormally (OOM in delta encode, or a WindowTimer throw), reaches its finally, fails the queue at :246, then enters closeDelegateQuietly() and is inside delegate.close() == LeaseManager.release(). release() takes lock.tryLock() (interrupt-insensitive) and proceeds into releaseLocked(), which issues a store write. close() now arrives and fires committer.interrupt(). On an NIO/S3 backend that write dies with ClosedByInterruptException; if the lock was contended instead, release() is in takeOrFail and tryLock(ttl, NANOSECONDS) throws InterruptedException at once. Either way the IOException is swallowed by the new catch (Throwable) at :303 and logged, close()'s join returns, claimDelegateClose() at :473 returns FALSE, close() skips the delegate and returns with no exception. Net: the pod's shutdown reports success while the lease is held to its TTL, and the closing caller is told nothing. R7b's reordering widened this window by design rather than creating it -- callers are now freed BEFORE the release runs, so the caller that has just been handed 'the commit batcher terminated abnormally' is the natural trigger for the close that lands inside the release; before the reordering no caller was awake during it. The ERROR log at :304 does tell an operator, which is why this is minor and not major, and the new comment at :464-472 already records the 'this caller does not learn it at all' half. What is not recorded is that close() itself is a CAUSE of the release failing, not merely a bystander -- the same hazard close() defends itself against at :440/:489 it inflicts on the committer.
findings.note: Related and smaller: the comment at :294-296 says LocalSequencer.close 'reaches BoundedLock.takeOrFail' flatly, but LeaseManager.release tries the non-blocking, interrupt-insensitive lock.tryLock() first and only falls through to takeOrFail under contention -- the qualification the close() comment at :480 carries and this one drops. The fix is still right (releaseLocked's store write is itself interrupt-sensitive), but the stated mechanism overstates its own frequency, and baselines/review.txt inherits the overstatement verbatim.

findings.title: the join-timeout WARNING promises an action that the CAS twenty lines below may skip
findings.failure_scenario: The WARNING reads 'the commit batcher did not stop within 10s; closing the delegate with a commit possibly still in flight'. It is emitted whenever !stopped, but the delegate close at :473-475 is conditional on claimDelegateClose(). Case: the committer died abnormally, claimed the close, and is stuck in a slow LeaseManager.release (takeOrFail waits up to ttl). close() joins for 10 s, times out, logs this WARNING -- and then does NOT close the delegate, because the CAS was already taken. An operator reading the log concludes the lease was released here and reasons about the I2 fork the message names; in fact nothing was closed on this path and whether the lease came back at all depends on the committer's swallowed outcome. The same message is also emitted when join() was INTERRUPTED rather than timed out (the catch at :444 leaves stopped == false), where '10s' is simply false: the wait may have lasted microseconds.

findings.title: the margin claim added to justify the 120 ms -> 300 ms change is true of one bound and overstated for the other -- and the overstated one guards the cost mutation
findings.failure_scenario: The comment asserts '300 ms RATHER THAN 120 ... a 4x mutation lands at 1200 ms and a 200 ms constant lands below the floor, so both bounds discriminate with ~400 ms of slack rather than tens of milliseconds', and baselines/review.txt cites this pair as the reason a minor was fixed rather than recorded. Arithmetic on the test's own constants: the ceiling case has 1200 ms against a 700 ms ceiling, ~500 ms of separation. The floor case does not: `() -> Thread.sleep(200)` yields an elapsed span of 200 ms plus BatchingSequencer construction, one MemoryBinStore putIfAbsent with a double encode, and close()'s interrupt+join, all of which are inside the measured window because `before` is taken before the try -- call it 210-260 ms against a 300 ms floor, so ~50-90 ms of separation, not ~400. That is the bound guarding the mutation the baseline entry itself calls '25x the PUT rate ... a cost defect wearing a minor's clothes', so it is the one whose margin matters most, and it is the thinner of the two by roughly 5x. Consequence if the claim is believed: on a loaded machine (two review trees plus the author's suite, which is the normal state here) a 200 ms-constant mutation can land above 300 ms and survive the very assertion added to kill it, while the comment tells the next reader the margin is generous. I did not measure this -- it is arithmetic on the constants in the diff, and measuring it is the test reviewer's call.
